metadata.title: Ideal gas: volume, temperature and pressure move together
metadata.subject: Chemistry
metadata.objective: Connect pressure, volume and temperature changes for a fixed amount of gas.
misconceptions: Pressure and temperature are the same quantity
The volume of a gas can change by itself, without work
expectedUnderstanding: For a fixed amount of gas, P, V and T are linked: P times V divided by T stays constant, 0.0821 in these units for one mole.
Halving V at fixed T doubles P; doubling T at fixed V doubles P; the two effects combine, as at 3 litres and 600 kelvin where P is 16 atmospheres.
The mechanism is the fixed number of molecules: less room or faster molecules mean more collisions with each patch of wall per second.
The volume changes only because the piston moves, which is work done on or by the gas; this is the ideal-gas model and says nothing about real gases at high pressure.

primitives.text: Ideal gas: squeeze the volume or heat it, and watch the pressure respond
volume V (1 to 3 L): the slider moves the piston
ideal gas, fixed amount: P·V = n·R·T; here n = 1 mol, so P·V/T = 0.0821

checkpoints.title: What is held fixed
checkpoints.body: The cylinder is sealed and the amount of gas does not change. Which quantity does the left slider change, and what happens to the piston when it moves?

checkpoints.title: Half the room
checkpoints.body: V fell from 2 litres to 1 at 300 kelvin and the bar climbed from 12 to 25 atmospheres. Why do the same molecules strike the walls twice as often per unit area?

checkpoints.title: Twice the temperature
checkpoints.body: Now the volume is back at 2 litres and T rose from 300 to 600 kelvin; the pressure doubled again. Is pressure the same thing as temperature, or does it rise because the molecules move faster?

checkpoints.title: Which product is constant
checkpoints.body: From 2 litres and 600 kelvin to 3 litres and 600 kelvin the pressure fell to 16 atmospheres. Which quantity stayed fixed: P, P times V, or P times V over T?

narration.text: One mole of gas in a cylinder with a piston. The blue dots are the molecules: the number never changes, only the room they have.
Push the piston in and you do work on the gas: the volume falls to 1 litre while the temperature stays at 300 kelvin.
The pressure doubles, from 12 to 25 atmospheres. Same molecules, half the room, twice as many collisions with each patch of wall every second.
Draw the piston back out and the pressure returns. At a fixed temperature the product P times V stays constant.
Now heat it instead: 300 to 600 kelvin at fixed volume, and the pressure doubles again. Twice the temperature, twice the pressure.
Move the piston to 3 litres while it stays at 600 kelvin and the pressure settles at 16 atmospheres. P times V over T is 0.0821 all along: that is the quantity the gas keeps.

fallback.text: Static figure. A cylinder from 1 litre to 3 litres with a piston and the same six molecules drawn in it, and a pressure bar read against a printed scale from 0 to 40 atmospheres. Four states are tabulated beside it. State 1: V = 2 L, T = 300 K, P = 12.3 atm. State 2: V = 1 L, T = 300 K, P = 24.6 atm (half the volume, double the pressure). State 3: V = 2 L, T = 600 K, P = 24.6 atm (double the temperature, double the pressure). State 4: V = 3 L, T = 600 K, P = 16.4 atm. In every row P times V divided by T is 0.0821, the value of R for one mole. Caption: with the amount fixed, P V over T is constant; the volume changes only because the piston moves, which is work.

accessibility.alt: A cylinder with a piston and three blue molecules inside, and to its right a vertical bar for pressure read against a printed scale from 10 to 40 atmospheres. As the volume slider moves the piston left, the blue region and the ring of molecules compress and the pressure bar rises; as the temperature slider rises, the pressure bar rises while the piston stays put. The bar is 12 atmospheres at 2 litres and 300 kelvin, 25 atmospheres at 1 litre and 300 kelvin, 25 at 2 litres and 600 kelvin, and 16 at 3 litres and 600 kelvin.
